summary: A 1971 first cut at a proposed Telnet protocol, by J. T. Melvin and R. W. Watson. Telnet lets a user at one computer act as a terminal on another. It is an early proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: This early proposal describes how a terminal at one site could provide interactive access to a remote server. It sketches ways to handle echoing, character codes and line controls while noting that several issues still need study.

subtitle: An early Telnet proposal for making a remote terminal behave like one attached to a server host.

tldr.problem: Users needed interactive access to remote network systems despite differences in terminal hardware, character handling, echoing and line behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal treats the user's terminal as logically equivalent to a terminal attached to the server and sketches conventions for echoing, character codes and line controls.
tldr.outcome: The authors call this a first cut, expect the final Telnet protocol to differ, and leave several issues for further study.

today: RFC 97 is an early proposal whose text says the final Telnet protocol will differ. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Telnet Proposal
sections.content:
The authors describe Telnet as a process at a user's site that lets a typewriter-like terminal access an interactive service at a remote server over the ARPA Network. Their immediate motivation is access to the Network Information Center's online system.

They call this a first cut and expect the final protocol to differ. They hope that discussion and a survey of terminal requirements will lead to an initial network Telnet protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet is meant to let a user work interactively with a remote system through a local terminal. This document is an early proposal, not a final specification.

sections.title: Terminal and Echoing Differences
sections.content:
The basic goal is for a terminal used over the network to appear logically equivalent to one connected directly to the server. The proposal considers whether users can generate the codes the server expects, escape to local or server functions, and connect line-at-a-time terminals to character-at-a-time systems.

It describes three echoing cases: the server echoes each character, the user site echoes each character, or the user site echoes a line. It also raises how to handle tab, form feed, line feed and carriage return characters, and whether network message boundaries can remain invisible to user processes.
sections.plainLanguage: Different terminals handle typing, echoing and line endings differently. Telnet needs conventions so the remote system can work with those differences.

sections.title: Proposed Character and Echo Conventions
sections.content:
The server initially assumes the user site performs echoing unless told otherwise. The server expects the character set used by its directly connected terminals; the authors recommend supporting at least 128 ASCII characters. The user's Telnet may need multi-character sequences to generate upper- and lowercase letters and control codes.

The authors propose sending a carriage return as CR over the network, converting it back if the user's terminal system changes it to CRLF or another end-of-line code. They also discuss an end-of-stream character to distinguish network transmission boundaries from end-of-line behavior. Line-at-a-time systems, interrupts and escape handling need further study.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal tries to keep character meanings consistent between the user's terminal and the remote server. It leaves some line and interrupt behavior unresolved.

sections.title: Appendix: Access to the NIC
sections.content:
The appendix applies the proposal to the Network Information Center's NLS system. It describes connection setup using the NIC logger at socket 1 and two connections for communication.

The first 8 bits received by the NIC identify an 8-bit ASCII stream as 00000001. The appendix also describes character handling, an interrupt-attention code presently set to DEL (ASCII 177), and the assumption that echoing is performed at the user site unless the NIC is told otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix gives a specific example for connecting to the NIC system. It describes the socket, data type and character conventions that the example uses.
